abstract: The stereotyped spread of tau pathology through connected brain regions is accompanied by striking differences in the vulnerability of individual neuronal populations, pointing to cell-intrinsic determinants of susceptibility. Using a combination of computational APR analysis, in vitro and cellular aggregation assays, and quantitative proteomics of human postmortem brain, we identify the splicing factor TRA2B as an endogenous modifier of this susceptibility. TRA2B enhances the activity of patient-derived tau seeds, promotes tau pathology in vivo, and progressively redistributes from the nucleus into insoluble tau-associated material in Alzheimers disease brain. Mechanistically, TRA2B contains two aggregation-prone regions (APRs) homologous to tau nucleation sites that are required for tau interaction and seeding enhancement. Yet this activity is not constitutive: isolated TRA2B APRs promote aggregation, whereas the full-length protein can inhibit, amplify or have little effect on tau aggregation depending on protein state and seeding context. Perturbation of the regulatory RS2 region switches TRA2B away from its amplifying state, revealing that its sequence-encoded aggregation potential is regulatable. Thus, TRA2B acts as a latent tau amplifier, providing a mechanism by which the neuronal proteome can tune cellular susceptibility to the propagation of pathological tau.
